title: Reproductive Hormones & Bone
summary: Estrogens, progestins, androgens, their modulators, and drugs for bone health.

lessons.title: Estrogens, Progestins and Contraception

levels.kid: Your body has messenger chemicals called hormones. Two important ones are estrogen and progesterone. They travel in the blood and tell different parts of the body what to do, a bit like a coach sending signals to players. Estrogen helps build strong bones and helps the body grow up during the teen years. Progesterone helps get the body ready for a baby. Doctors can make copies of these hormones as medicines. Some of these medicines are used to plan when to have a family, and some help women whose own hormones are low. Like every medicine, they can have side effects, so a doctor checks if they are safe for each person first.
levels.hs:
**Estrogens** (mainly estradiol) and **progestins** (progesterone and its synthetic relatives) are steroid hormones. Because they are fat-soluble, they cross cell membranes and bind receptors inside the cell that switch genes on or off.

**Natural roles:** estrogen drives puberty changes, keeps bones strong and affects cholesterol and blood clotting. Progesterone prepares the lining of the uterus and keeps it stable.

**Control:** the hypothalamus releases GnRH, which makes the pituitary release LH and FSH. These act on the ovaries. Steroids feed back to turn this system down.

**Hormonal contraception** uses that feedback. Combined pills (an estrogen plus a progestin) suppress LH and FSH so no egg is released (ovulation is blocked). Progestins also thicken cervical mucus. Progestin-only methods include pills, implants and hormonal IUDs.

**Other uses:** menopausal hormone therapy, treating heavy or painful periods, and treating low hormone states.

**Main risk:** estrogen makes the liver produce more clotting factors, so it raises the risk of blood clots (venous thromboembolism). This risk is higher in smokers over 35 and people with certain migraines. Some seizure and TB drugs speed up hormone breakdown and make pills less effective.
levels.college:
**Receptors.** Estrogens act on ERα and ERβ, ligand-activated nuclear receptors that dimerize, bind estrogen response elements and recruit coactivators (SRC family) or corepressors. A membrane GPCR, GPER, mediates some rapid effects. Progesterone acts on PR-A and PR-B; PR-A can repress PR-B and ER activity, which partly explains progestin antagonism of estrogen-driven endometrial growth.

**Agents.** Ethinyl estradiol has a 17α-ethinyl group that blocks hepatic first-pass oxidation, giving high oral potency and a strong hepatic effect. Estradiol is used transdermally or orally in menopausal therapy. Progestins are grouped by structure: 19-nortestosterone derivatives (norethindrone, levonorgestrel, desogestrel), which have some androgenic activity; drospirenone, a spironolactone analog with antimineralocorticoid action; and pregnane derivatives (medroxyprogesterone acetate).

**Contraceptive mechanism.** Combined hormonal contraception suppresses the mid-cycle LH surge through negative feedback on GnRH pulses and pituitary responsiveness, preventing follicle maturation and ovulation. Progestins also thicken cervical mucus and make the endometrium unreceptive. The levonorgestrel IUD acts mostly locally; the etonogestrel implant reliably suppresses ovulation.

**Adverse effects.** Estrogen raises hepatic synthesis of clotting factors, angiotensinogen, SHBG and TBG. VTE risk rises with dose, with smoking, thrombophilias (factor V Leiden) and the postpartum period. Absolute contraindications to estrogen include migraine with aura (stroke risk), prior VTE, active breast cancer and smokers over 35. Unopposed estrogen in a patient with a uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia, so a progestin is added.

**Interactions.** CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) lower contraceptive efficacy. Estrogen induces glucuronidation of lamotrigine, lowering its levels.
levels.phd:
**Why ethinyl estradiol is so hepatic.** Oral delivery exposes the liver to high portal concentrations; the ethinyl group slows inactivation, so hepatic ER signaling dominates. This explains greater increases in SHBG, angiotensinogen and procoagulant factors with ethinyl estradiol than with transdermal estradiol, and why newer combined products pair progestins with estradiol or estetrol. Estetrol, a fetal liver estrogen, shows weaker hepatic effects in early studies, possibly because it acts as an agonist at nuclear ERα but antagonizes membrane-initiated ERα signaling; the full clinical significance is still being studied.

**Progestin androgenicity and VTE.** Epidemiological studies associated desogestrel, gestodene and drospirenone combinations with modestly higher VTE risk than levonorgestrel combinations. One hypothesis is that androgenic progestins partly offset ethinyl estradiol's hepatic effects; activated protein C resistance assays support this, though confounding by prescribing patterns was debated. The absolute risk remains far lower than in pregnancy and the postpartum period, a point often lost.

**Receptor pharmacology.** Selective progesterone receptor modulators such as ulipristal act as mixed agonist/antagonists at PR; ulipristal delays follicular rupture even when the LH surge has begun, which is why it remains effective later in the follicular phase than levonorgestrel emergency contraception. Mifepristone is a PR and glucocorticoid receptor antagonist.

**Menopausal therapy and timing.** The Women's Health Initiative found increased breast cancer, stroke and VTE with conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone in older women. Later reanalyses support the timing hypothesis: started near menopause, estrogen may have a neutral or favorable vascular profile, while in established atherosclerosis it may destabilize plaque. Transdermal routes avoid the first-pass procoagulant signal.
levels.expert:
**Choosing safely.** Clinicians use the CDC Medical Eligibility Criteria (US MEC), which grades each method by condition from 1 (no restriction) to 4 (unacceptable risk). Key estrogen category 4 conditions: migraine with aura, history of VTE or known thrombophilia, uncontrolled hypertension, smoking over 35, recent major surgery with immobilization, complicated valvular disease and current breast cancer. Progestin-only methods and the copper IUD are usually the fallback when estrogen is unsafe.

**Drug interactions that matter.** Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, oxcarbazepine, topiramate at higher exposures) and rifampin reduce efficacy of pills, patches, rings and the implant; the IUDs and depot medroxyprogesterone are not meaningfully affected. Ask about St John's wort, which patients often omit. The lamotrigine interaction is two-way in practice: starting a combined pill can drop lamotrigine levels and provoke seizures, and the hormone-free week can cause a rebound in levels with toxicity.

**Neurology overlap.** For a future neurosurgeon: estrogen-containing methods raise stroke risk in migraine with aura, and estrogen is a known risk factor for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. A young patient with a new severe headache, papilledema or seizures on a combined pill should prompt venous imaging.

**Pitfalls.**
- Unopposed estrogen in someone with a uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia; always pair with a progestin.
- Depot medroxyprogesterone reduces bone mineral density, mostly reversible after stopping.
- Before any elective surgery with high clot risk, estrogen methods are often paused in advance per local protocols.
- New unilateral leg swelling, chest pain or neurological signs in a patient on estrogen are a clot until proven otherwise.

keyPoints: Estrogens act on ERα/ERβ; progestins on PR (nuclear receptors that change gene expression)
Combined contraception blocks the LH surge and ovulation by negative feedback
Estrogen raises hepatic clotting factors: VTE is the key risk
Migraine with aura, prior VTE and smoking over 35 contraindicate estrogen
Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine) reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy
Unopposed estrogen with a uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia

test.q: How do combined hormonal contraceptives mainly prevent pregnancy?
choices: They destroy eggs in the ovary
They suppress the LH surge, blocking ovulation
test.explain: Estrogen plus progestin feedback suppresses GnRH pulses and the mid-cycle LH surge, so no follicle ruptures.

test.q: The most important serious risk of estrogen-containing contraception is:
test.explain: Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of clotting factors, raising the risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism.

test.q: Which condition is an absolute contraindication to estrogen-containing methods?
test.explain: Migraine with aura plus estrogen raises ischemic stroke risk, so estrogen is avoided.

test.q: Why is a progestin added to estrogen in menopausal therapy for someone with a uterus?
test.explain: Unopposed estrogen stimulates endometrial growth; progestins oppose this and lower cancer risk.

test.q: Which drug lowers the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptive pills?
test.explain: Rifampin strongly induces CYP3A4, speeding breakdown of ethinyl estradiol and progestins.

test.q: Drospirenone is unusual among progestins because it:
choices: Is given only as an injection
test.explain: Drospirenone is a spironolactone analog, so it opposes aldosterone, which can raise potassium.

test.q: Which feature makes ethinyl estradiol orally potent?
choices: A sulfur atom in ring A
It is a protein too large to digest
A 17α-ethinyl group that slows hepatic metabolism
test.explain: The ethinyl group blocks first-pass oxidation at C17, so much more survives oral dosing.

test.q: Name the pituitary hormone whose mid-cycle surge triggers ovulation (abbreviation).
test.explain: The LH surge triggers follicle rupture; combined pills suppress it.

test.q: Estrogens act mainly on nuclear receptors called ER-alpha and ER-___.
test.explain: ERα and ERβ are the two classic estrogen receptors with different tissue distributions.

test.q: Which antiseizure drug's levels drop when a combined estrogen pill is started (it is glucuronidated)?
test.explain: Estrogen induces UGT enzymes that glucuronidate lamotrigine, lowering its levels.

test.q: Progestins thicken cervical ___, adding to the contraceptive effect.
test.explain: Thick cervical mucus blocks sperm movement, a key effect of progestin-only methods.

kidTest.q: What are hormones?
kidTest.explain: Hormones carry signals around the body, like a coach sending signals.

kidTest.q: Estrogen helps keep which part of the body strong?
kidTest.explain: Estrogen helps build and protect bones.

kidTest.q: Who should check if a hormone medicine is safe for someone?
kidTest.explain: Doctors check health history because these medicines can have side effects.

kidTest.q: Can doctors make copies of hormones as medicines?
kidTest.explain: Many hormone medicines are copies of the body's own hormones.

kidTest.q: Estrogen and ___ are two important hormones in this lesson.
kidTest.explain: Progesterone helps get the body ready for a baby.

advancedTest.q: A patient taking lamotrigine starts a combined pill with a hormone-free week. What pattern is most likely?
choices: Lower lamotrigine during active pills, higher during the hormone-free week
Lamotrigine levels rise only when the pill starts
advancedTest.explain: Estrogen induces glucuronidation; levels fall on active pills and rebound during the break, risking seizures then toxicity.

advancedTest.q: Why can ulipristal still work later in the follicular phase than levonorgestrel emergency contraception?
choices: It delays follicular rupture even after the LH surge has started
It acts on the uterus only
advancedTest.explain: As a PR modulator it can postpone follicle rupture after LH begins rising, when levonorgestrel no longer works.

advancedTest.q: Compared with oral ethinyl estradiol, transdermal estradiol causes:
choices: Smaller increases in hepatic clotting factors and SHBG
advancedTest.explain: Transdermal delivery avoids high portal concentrations, so the hepatic procoagulant signal is weaker.

advancedTest.q: A young woman on a combined pill develops headache, papilledema and seizures. Which diagnosis must be excluded urgently?
advancedTest.explain: Estrogen is a risk factor for CVST; papilledema and seizures point to it and need venous imaging.

lessons.title: SERMs and Aromatase Inhibitors

levels.kid: Some cancers in the breast grow faster when estrogen touches them, like a plant that grows faster with fertilizer. Doctors have two clever ways to stop the fertilizer. The first kind of medicine sits in the estrogen's parking spot in the cancer cell, so estrogen can't park there. The funny part is that in other places, like bones, the same medicine acts like estrogen and helps. The second kind of medicine stops the body from making much estrogen in the first place. It blocks a factory worker, an enzyme, that turns other hormones into estrogen. Both kinds help stop the cancer from coming back.
levels.hs:
**SERMs** (selective estrogen receptor modulators) bind the estrogen receptor but act differently in different tissues: like estrogen in some tissues (agonist) and against estrogen in others (antagonist).

- **Tamoxifen:** blocks estrogen in breast tissue, so it treats and prevents estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer. But it acts like estrogen in the uterus (raising endometrial cancer risk) and in bone (protecting bone).
- **Raloxifene:** blocks estrogen in breast and uterus but acts like estrogen in bone, so it is used for osteoporosis and to lower breast cancer risk.
- **Clomiphene:** blocks estrogen feedback in the hypothalamus, raising FSH and LH to trigger ovulation in infertility.

Both tamoxifen and raloxifene raise the risk of blood clots and can cause hot flashes.

**Aromatase inhibitors** (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) block **aromatase**, the enzyme that converts androgens into estrogens. After menopause, most estrogen comes from this conversion in fat and other tissues, so these drugs are used for ER-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. They cause bone loss and joint pain because estrogen falls everywhere.
levels.college:
**Tissue selectivity.** A SERM's effect depends on the receptor conformation it induces, which ER subtype dominates, and which coactivators and corepressors the cell expresses. ERα has two activation functions: ligand-independent AF-1 and ligand-dependent AF-2. Estradiol positions helix 12 over the ligand pocket, completing the AF-2 coactivator groove. Tamoxifen's bulky side chain displaces helix 12 so AF-2 is blocked; in cells where AF-1 drives transcription and coactivators such as SRC-1 are abundant (endometrium), tamoxifen is a partial agonist.

**Agents.**
- **Tamoxifen** is a prodrug, converted by CYP2D6 (and CYP3A4) to endoxifen and 4-hydroxytamoxifen, which bind ER far more strongly. Uses: adjuvant therapy for ER-positive breast cancer (pre- and postmenopausal) and risk reduction. Adverse effects: hot flashes, VTE, endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, cataracts.
- **Raloxifene**: antagonist in breast and endometrium, agonist in bone; reduces vertebral fractures and invasive breast cancer risk; raises VTE and leg cramps.
- **Bazedoxifene** paired with conjugated estrogens (a tissue-selective estrogen complex) protects the endometrium without a progestin.
- **Fulvestrant** is a pure antagonist and selective ER degrader (SERD).

**Aromatase inhibitors.** Aromatase (CYP19A1) converts androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to estradiol. Anastrozole and letrozole are reversible nonsteroidal triazoles; exemestane is a steroidal irreversible inactivator. They are standard adjuvant therapy in postmenopausal ER-positive disease and are used in premenopausal women only with ovarian suppression, because falling estrogen would otherwise increase gonadotropins and ovarian output. Adverse effects: arthralgia, bone loss and fractures, and lipid changes.
levels.phd:
**Structural basis of SERM pharmacology.** Crystal structures of ERα ligand-binding domains (Brzozowski 1997, Shiau 1998) showed agonists sealing helix 12 across the pocket, while raloxifene and 4-hydroxytamoxifen relocate helix 12 into the coactivator groove, mimicking an LxxLL motif and occluding it. Agonism by tamoxifen in endometrium reflects AF-1 activity, tethered transcription through AP-1 and Sp1 sites, and high SRC-1 levels. Raloxifene's different side chain geometry and interaction with Asp351 make it a stronger antagonist in uterus.

**Endocrine resistance.** Acquired resistance often involves activating ESR1 ligand-binding domain mutations (Y537S, D538G), selected under aromatase inhibitor therapy because they stabilize the agonist conformation without ligand. These mutants remain partially sensitive to SERDs. Oral SERDs such as elacestrant have shown benefit in ESR1-mutant advanced disease, and detecting ESR1 mutations in circulating tumor DNA now guides therapy. Growth factor crosstalk (HER2, PI3K-AKT-mTOR) and CDK4/6-driven cell cycle escape explain why CDK4/6 inhibitors combined with endocrine therapy changed outcomes in advanced disease.

**Pharmacogenomics.** Because endoxifen formation depends on CYP2D6, poor metabolizers and patients on strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine, bupropion) have lower endoxifen. Retrospective associations with recurrence led to debate; prospective data were inconsistent, but guidelines (CPIC) suggest alternative endocrine therapy for poor metabolizers where appropriate, and most clinicians avoid strong CYP2D6 inhibitors with tamoxifen.

**Aromatase biology.** CYP19A1 uses tissue-specific promoters (placenta, gonads, adipose, bone, brain), so local estrogen synthesis persists after menopause. In the brain, local aromatization of testosterone contributes to neural estrogen signaling, part of why aromatase inhibitors can affect mood and cognition in some patients.
levels.expert:
**How oncologists choose.** For hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer, the main decision is menopausal status. Postmenopausal patients usually get an aromatase inhibitor, sometimes switched from or to tamoxifen. Premenopausal patients get tamoxifen, or ovarian suppression with a GnRH agonist plus an aromatase inhibitor or tamoxifen when risk is higher. Adjuvant endocrine therapy usually lasts years, and adherence is a major issue because joint pain and hot flashes are common reasons to stop.

**Monitoring and pitfalls.**
- **Tamoxifen:** any abnormal uterine bleeding after menopause needs evaluation for endometrial cancer. Check medication lists for strong CYP2D6 inhibitors; venlafaxine or other low-interaction options are usually preferred when an antidepressant is needed for hot flashes or mood.
- **VTE:** tamoxifen and raloxifene raise risk; they are usually stopped ahead of prolonged immobility or major surgery per local protocols.
- **Aromatase inhibitors:** baseline and follow-up bone density scans, vitamin D and calcium status, and often a bisphosphonate or denosumab, which also has adjuvant benefit in some postmenopausal patients.
- An aromatase inhibitor alone in a premenopausal patient is ineffective and can stimulate the ovaries; confirm menopause or add ovarian suppression.

**Fertility.** Clomiphene and letrozole are both used for ovulation induction; letrozole is now often first line in polycystic ovary syndrome because trials showed higher live birth rates. Monitoring for multiple follicles is essential.

**Neuro angle.** Patients with brain metastases from breast cancer still need systemic therapy; endocrine agents penetrate the CNS variably, and the treatment plan is coordinated between neurosurgery, radiation oncology and medical oncology.

keyPoints: SERMs are agonists in some tissues and antagonists in others
Tamoxifen: breast antagonist, uterine agonist (endometrial cancer risk), raises VTE
Raloxifene: bone agonist, breast/uterine antagonist; used for osteoporosis
Tamoxifen is a prodrug activated by CYP2D6 to endoxifen
Aromatase inhibitors block androgen-to-estrogen conversion; used after menopause
AIs cause bone loss and arthralgia

test.q: A SERM is best described as a drug that:
choices: Acts as an estrogen agonist in some tissues and antagonist in others
test.explain: Selectivity comes from tissue-specific receptor conformations and coregulators.

test.q: Which tamoxifen effect explains the endometrial cancer risk?
choices: Partial agonist activity in the uterus
test.explain: In endometrium tamoxifen behaves like estrogen, stimulating growth.

test.q: Raloxifene is mainly used for:
choices: Osteoporosis and breast cancer risk reduction
test.explain: It is an agonist in bone and an antagonist in breast.

test.q: Aromatase converts:
test.explain: Aromatase (CYP19A1) converts androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to estradiol.

test.q: Why are aromatase inhibitors alone not used in premenopausal women?
choices: The ovaries respond to falling estrogen by producing more
test.explain: Lower estrogen removes feedback, raising gonadotropins and ovarian output; ovarian suppression is needed.

test.q: A common adverse effect of aromatase inhibitors is:
test.explain: Estrogen deprivation in bone and joints causes osteoporosis and arthralgia.

test.q: Clomiphene helps ovulation by:
choices: Blocking estrogen feedback in the hypothalamus
test.explain: Blocking hypothalamic ER makes the brain sense low estrogen, increasing GnRH, FSH and LH.

test.q: Name the active tamoxifen metabolite formed mainly by CYP2D6.
test.explain: Endoxifen binds ER far more strongly than tamoxifen.

test.q: Fulvestrant is a selective estrogen receptor ___ (SERD).
test.explain: It is a pure antagonist that causes ER degradation.

test.q: Which enzyme do anastrozole and letrozole block?
test.explain: They are reversible nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitors.

test.q: Which side effect do tamoxifen and raloxifene share?
choices: Increased risk of venous blood clots
test.explain: Both have estrogen-like hepatic effects that raise VTE risk.

kidTest.q: Some breast cancers grow faster with which hormone?
kidTest.explain: These cancers use estrogen like fertilizer.

kidTest.q: One medicine type sits in estrogen's parking spot. What does that do?
kidTest.explain: If the spot is taken, estrogen can't send its signal.

kidTest.q: The other medicine type works by:
choices: Stopping the body from making much estrogen
kidTest.explain: It blocks the enzyme that makes estrogen.

kidTest.q: The enzyme that makes estrogen is called ___.
kidTest.explain: Aromatase turns other hormones into estrogen.

kidTest.q: Can the same medicine help bones and block estrogen in cancer?
kidTest.explain: These medicines act differently in different body parts.

advancedTest.q: A patient on tamoxifen starts paroxetine for hot flashes. What is the concern?
choices: Strong CYP2D6 inhibition lowers endoxifen formation
advancedTest.explain: Paroxetine strongly inhibits CYP2D6, reducing tamoxifen activation; venlafaxine is usually preferred.

advancedTest.q: Activating ESR1 ligand-binding domain mutations (e.g., Y537S) are typically selected by:
advancedTest.explain: Estrogen deprivation selects for mutant receptors that are active without ligand.

choices: It covalently binds the DNA domain
Its side chain displaces helix 12 into the coactivator groove
advancedTest.explain: Helix 12 repositioning occludes the coactivator binding surface.

lessons.title: Androgens and Antiandrogens

levels.kid: Testosterone is a hormone that helps boys' bodies grow up: deeper voices, bigger muscles and stronger bones. Some people's bodies don't make enough, and doctors can give them a copy of it. But sometimes testosterone causes trouble. A gland in older men, the prostate, can grow too big, and some prostate cancers grow faster when testosterone is around, like a fire getting more wood. Doctors can stop this in a few ways: block the spot where testosterone attaches, stop the body from making it, or stop it from turning into a stronger form. Taking away the wood makes the fire smaller.
levels.hs:
**Androgens** are hormones like **testosterone**, made mainly by the testes (and a little by the adrenal glands). They drive male puberty, muscle and bone growth, red blood cell production and hair growth.

**Testosterone and DHT:** in some tissues (prostate, skin, hair follicles), the enzyme **5-alpha-reductase** converts testosterone into **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)**, which is more potent.

**Medical use of testosterone:** replacement in **hypogonadism** (when the body makes too little). Doctors monitor red blood cell count (it can get too high) and the prostate.

**Blocking androgens:**
- **5-alpha-reductase inhibitors** (finasteride, dutasteride): shrink an enlarged prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia) and treat hair loss.
- **Androgen receptor blockers** (bicalutamide, enzalutamide): used in prostate cancer.
- **Abiraterone:** blocks an enzyme needed to make androgens anywhere in the body, including the adrenal glands and the tumor itself.
- **Spironolactone:** a diuretic that also blocks androgen receptors, used for acne and excess hair growth in women.

Lowering androgens causes hot flashes, tiredness, weaker bones and breast tissue growth.
levels.college:
**Biosynthesis and action.** Testosterone is made in Leydig cells under LH stimulation. CYP17A1 (17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase) is the gateway to androgens from pregnenolone and progesterone. Testosterone acts directly on the androgen receptor (AR) or is converted to DHT by 5α-reductase type 2 (prostate, genital skin) and type 1 (skin, liver), or to estradiol by aromatase. DHT binds AR with higher affinity and dissociates more slowly. AR is a nuclear receptor; ligand binding releases heat shock proteins, causes nuclear translocation, dimerization and binding to androgen response elements (e.g., the PSA gene, KLK3).

**Testosterone therapy.** Formulations include transdermal gels, injectable esters and others; oral 17α-alkylated androgens are avoided because of hepatotoxicity. Adverse effects: erythrocytosis, acne, gynecomastia via aromatization, suppression of the HPG axis with reduced sperm production, and fluid retention.

**Antiandrogens.**
- **5α-reductase inhibitors**: finasteride (type 2 selective) and dutasteride (types 1 and 2) shrink the prostate over months and lower serum PSA by roughly half, which must be accounted for in screening.
- **First-generation AR antagonists** (flutamide, bicalutamide) can become partial agonists with certain AR mutations.
- **Second-generation AR inhibitors** (enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide) block ligand binding, nuclear translocation and DNA binding. Enzalutamide lowers seizure threshold and is a strong CYP3A4 inducer; darolutamide penetrates the brain less.
- **Abiraterone** irreversibly inhibits CYP17A1, blocking adrenal, gonadal and intratumoral androgen synthesis. Because cortisol falls and ACTH rises, mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalemia, edema) occurs, so it is given with prednisone.
- **Spironolactone** and **cyproterone** block AR for hirsutism and acne.
levels.phd:
**Castration-resistant prostate cancer is still AR-driven.** After androgen deprivation, tumors adapt through AR amplification and overexpression, ligand-binding domain mutations (T878A, which converts flutamide and progesterone into agonists; F877L, linked to enzalutamide agonism), intratumoral steroidogenesis via AKR1C3 and HSD3B1 variants, and constitutively active splice variants such as AR-V7, which lack the ligand-binding domain entirely and therefore escape all ligand-binding-domain antagonists. Detection of AR-V7 in circulating tumor cells predicted poor response to enzalutamide and abiraterone in some studies. Glucocorticoid receptor upregulation can substitute for AR at some target genes.

**New modalities.** Because AR-V7 lacks the ligand pocket, efforts target the N-terminal domain or degrade AR. PROTACs link an AR ligand to an E3 ligase recruiter (cereblon or VHL), causing ubiquitination and degradation; early trials showed activity especially in tumors with certain AR ligand-binding mutations. PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy (lutetium-177 PSMA-617) treats AR-independent or resistant disease.

**HSD3B1 genetics.** A gain-of-stability HSD3B1 variant (1245C) increases conversion of adrenal DHEA to potent androgens within the tumor and is associated with faster resistance to androgen deprivation, an example of germline genetics shaping somatic drug response.

**Brain and seizures.** Enzalutamide and apalutamide cross the blood-brain barrier and inhibit GABA-A receptors off target, which explains the seizure signal. Darolutamide's polar structure gives low brain penetration, so it is often preferred in patients with seizure risk or cognitive concerns.

**Bone.** Androgen deprivation removes both androgen and aromatized estrogen, accelerating bone loss; estrogen, not testosterone, is the main regulator of bone resorption in males as well.
levels.expert:
**Prostate cancer in practice.** Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is the backbone of advanced prostate cancer, using a GnRH agonist or antagonist. Adding an AR pathway inhibitor (abiraterone with prednisone, enzalutamide, apalutamide or darolutamide) improves survival in metastatic hormone-sensitive disease. PSA is followed for response, while imaging guides decisions about progression.

**Toxicity checklists.**
- **ADT:** hot flashes, fatigue, weight gain, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, anemia, bone loss. Baseline bone density, vitamin D, exercise, and a bisphosphonate or denosumab if risk is high.
- **Abiraterone:** must be given with a glucocorticoid. Monitor blood pressure, potassium and liver enzymes. Absorption increases markedly with food, so it is taken on an empty stomach, consistently.
- **Enzalutamide/apalutamide:** avoid in patients with seizure history where possible; enzalutamide induces CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19, which affects warfarin, some anticoagulants and many antiepileptics. Fall and fracture risk rises.
- **5α-reductase inhibitors:** double a measured PSA when interpreting screening on long-term therapy, and investigate a PSA that rises while on treatment.

**Testosterone replacement.** Diagnose hypogonadism with repeated morning testosterone levels plus symptoms, then find the cause (primary versus secondary). Monitor hematocrit and stop or adjust if erythrocytosis develops. Exogenous testosterone suppresses sperm production, an important counseling point for anyone planning a family; hCG or clomiphene are alternatives in secondary hypogonadism when fertility matters.

**Neurosurgery link.** Pituitary tumors (prolactinomas, nonfunctioning macroadenomas) are common causes of secondary hypogonadism. Low testosterone with low or normal LH should prompt pituitary evaluation, including prolactin and MRI when indicated.

keyPoints: 5α-reductase converts testosterone to the more potent DHT
Finasteride/dutasteride treat BPH and lower PSA by about half
Abiraterone inhibits CYP17A1 and is given with prednisone
Enzalutamide is a second-generation AR inhibitor that lowers seizure threshold
AR-V7 splice variants lack the ligand-binding domain and drive resistance
Testosterone therapy causes erythrocytosis and suppresses sperm production

test.q: Which enzyme converts testosterone to DHT?
test.explain: 5α-reductase (types 1 and 2) forms DHT in prostate, skin and hair follicles.

test.q: Finasteride is used for:
test.explain: By lowering DHT it shrinks the prostate over months.

test.q: Why is abiraterone given with prednisone?
choices: To prevent mineralocorticoid excess from rising ACTH
test.explain: CYP17A1 block lowers cortisol, ACTH rises and drives mineralocorticoid precursors; prednisone replaces cortisol and suppresses ACTH.

test.q: Which drug is an androgen receptor antagonist used in prostate cancer?
test.explain: Enzalutamide blocks ligand binding, nuclear translocation and DNA binding of AR.

test.q: A key lab to monitor during testosterone therapy is:
test.explain: Testosterone stimulates erythropoiesis and can cause erythrocytosis.

test.q: Spironolactone helps hirsutism because it:
test.explain: Besides blocking aldosterone it antagonizes AR in skin and hair follicles.

test.q: Long-term finasteride changes PSA how?
test.explain: Interpret PSA by roughly doubling the measured value on therapy.

test.q: Which enzyme does abiraterone inhibit? (format: CYP...)
test.explain: CYP17A1 is required for androgen synthesis in testes, adrenals and tumor.

test.q: Testosterone is made in ___ cells of the testis under LH stimulation.
test.explain: LH acts on Leydig cells; FSH acts on Sertoli cells.

test.q: Name the potent androgen made from testosterone in the prostate (abbreviation).
test.explain: DHT binds AR more tightly and dissociates more slowly.

test.q: Which effect is expected from androgen deprivation therapy?
test.explain: Loss of androgen and aromatized estrogen accelerates bone resorption.

kidTest.q: Which hormone helps boys' bodies grow up?
kidTest.explain: Testosterone deepens the voice and builds muscle and bone.

kidTest.q: Some prostate cancers grow faster with testosterone, like a fire with more:
kidTest.explain: Taking away testosterone is like taking away the wood.

kidTest.q: One way doctors stop testosterone is to:
choices: Block the spot where it attaches
kidTest.explain: Blocking the receptor stops the signal.

kidTest.q: The prostate is a ___ found in men.

lessons.title: GnRH Analogs

levels.kid: Deep in your brain is a control center that sends little pulses of a hormone called GnRH, like someone tapping a drum. Each tap tells another gland to release hormones that wake up the ovaries or testes. Here is the weird trick: if a medicine keeps the drum tapping nonstop instead of in beats, the gland gets tired of listening and stops answering. So a medicine that copies GnRH can actually turn the hormones off! Another kind of medicine simply covers the drum so nobody hears it. Doctors use these to slow some cancers and to pause puberty that starts much too early.
levels.hs:
The hypothalamus releases **GnRH** (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) in **pulses**, roughly every hour or two. Pulses tell the pituitary to release **LH** and **FSH**, which control the ovaries and testes.

**The pulse trick:** if GnRH is given steadily instead of in pulses, the pituitary stops responding. Its receptors are pulled inside the cell (downregulation), so LH, FSH and then testosterone or estrogen fall to very low levels.

**GnRH agonists** (leuprolide, goserelin, triptorelin) are given as long-acting depot injections or implants. At first they cause a **flare**: a surge in LH and testosterone for one to two weeks, before suppression starts.

**GnRH antagonists** (degarelix, relugolix, elagolix) block the receptor directly, so hormones fall within days with **no flare**.

**Uses:**
- Prostate cancer and some breast cancers
- Endometriosis and fibroids
- **Central precocious puberty** (puberty that starts too early)
- IVF, to control the timing of ovulation

**Side effects** come from low hormone levels: hot flashes, mood changes and bone loss.
levels.college:
**Physiology.** GnRH, a decapeptide, binds the GnRH receptor (GnRHR), a Gq-coupled GPCR on gonadotrophs, activating PLCβ, IP3/Ca²⁺ and PKC to drive LH and FSH synthesis and release. Pulse frequency encodes the output: fast pulses favor LH, slow pulses favor FSH. The mammalian type I GnRHR lacks a C-terminal tail, so it desensitizes and internalizes slowly at first, yet continuous exposure eventually uncouples signaling and reduces receptor and gonadotropin subunit expression.

**Agonists.** Substituting a D-amino acid at position 6 and modifying the C terminus protects against peptidase cleavage and increases receptor affinity and half-life. Initial stimulation produces a testosterone flare that can worsen bone pain, urinary obstruction or spinal cord compression in metastatic prostate cancer. An AR antagonist such as bicalutamide is started beforehand to block the flare's effects.

**Antagonists.**
- **Degarelix** (injectable peptide) suppresses testosterone within days. Injection site reactions are common.
- **Relugolix** (oral nonpeptide) is used in prostate cancer and, combined with estradiol and norethindrone add-back, for fibroids and endometriosis. A trial (HERO) reported fewer major cardiovascular events than leuprolide.
- **Elagolix** allows dose-dependent partial suppression for endometriosis pain.

**Uses.**
- **Central precocious puberty**: continuous agonists halt progression and preserve adult height potential. Puberty resumes after stopping.
- **IVF**: antagonists prevent a premature LH surge. An agonist trigger can replace hCG to induce final oocyte maturation, reducing ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome risk.
- **Add-back therapy** with low hormone exposure limits bone loss and vasomotor symptoms during long-term suppression.
levels.phd:
**Pulsatility as information.** The GnRH pulse generator is driven by arcuate KNDy neurons (kisspeptin, neurokinin B, dynorphin): neurokinin B stimulates and dynorphin inhibits kisspeptin release, producing synchronized episodes. Kisspeptin acts on KISS1R on GnRH neurons. Loss-of-function mutations in KISS1R or TACR3 cause hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and activating KISS1R or MKRN3 loss-of-function mutations cause central precocious puberty. This biology produced new drugs: neurokinin 3 receptor antagonists (fezolinetant) reduce menopausal hot flashes by quieting KNDy neurons that drive the thermoregulatory center, without directly replacing hormones.

**Decoding at the pituitary.** Gonadotrophs decode pulse frequency through differential activation of transcription factors (EGR1, CREB, ICER) and the follistatin/activin system. Slow pulses favor FSHβ transcription; fast pulses favor LHβ. Polycystic ovary syndrome features persistently rapid GnRH pulses with a high LH to FSH ratio.

**Desensitization mechanism.** Because type I GnRHR lacks the C-terminal tail that recruits arrestins in most GPCRs, desensitization by continuous agonist involves downstream uncoupling (reduced IP3 receptor and calcium signaling) and transcriptional suppression of gonadotropin subunits, rather than classic rapid receptor phosphorylation. This explains why suppression takes days to weeks and is preceded by a flare.

**Cardiovascular question.** Observational data linked ADT to cardiovascular events. One hypothesis is that agonists, but not antagonists, act on GnRH receptors on T cells and atherosclerotic plaque, or that FSH, which stays higher with agonists, promotes adipogenesis and atherogenesis. The HERO trial supported lower risk with relugolix, but confirmatory trials (PRONOUNCE) were inconclusive, so the issue remains open.
levels.expert:
**Prostate cancer with impending cord compression.** Never start a GnRH agonist alone in a man with vertebral metastases threatening the spinal cord or with severe outlet obstruction; the flare can cause paraplegia or retention. Options are an antagonist (immediate suppression without flare) or an agonist with an AR antagonist started first. True cord compression is an emergency for steroids and urgent neurosurgical or radiation assessment, with ADT started alongside.

**Monitoring.** Check castrate testosterone levels on therapy; a rising PSA with castrate testosterone defines castration resistance. Relugolix is oral, so adherence matters and it has interactions (P-gp inhibitors raise levels, strong inducers lower them). Testosterone recovers faster after stopping relugolix than after a depot agonist, which matters when intermittent therapy is planned.

**Pediatrics.** Central precocious puberty is defined by puberty onset before roughly age 8 in girls and 9 in boys with a pubertal LH response. Every boy and young child with central precocious puberty needs brain MRI, because hypothalamic hamartomas, gliomas and other lesions can be the cause; in girls the yield is lower but still considered by age and features. Treatment is with a long-acting agonist depot or implant, judged by growth velocity, bone age and stopping of physical progression.

**Gynecology.** For endometriosis and fibroids, long-term suppression causes bone loss, so add-back therapy is used when treatment lasts beyond several months. Uterine fibroids may be shrunk before surgery.

**IVF.** An agonist trigger in an antagonist cycle sharply lowers severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome risk in high responders because the endogenous LH surge it produces is short.

keyPoints: GnRH works only in pulses; continuous agonist exposure suppresses LH/FSH
Agonists (leuprolide, goserelin) cause an initial testosterone flare
Antagonists (degarelix, relugolix) suppress within days with no flare
Uses: prostate cancer, endometriosis, fibroids, central precocious puberty, IVF
Block the flare with an AR antagonist when metastases threaten the spinal cord
Long-term suppression causes bone loss; add-back therapy limits it

test.q: Why does continuous leuprolide lower testosterone?
choices: Continuous stimulation desensitizes pituitary GnRH receptors
test.explain: GnRH must pulse; steady exposure shuts down LH/FSH release.

test.q: What happens in the first one to two weeks of GnRH agonist therapy?
choices: A flare in LH and testosterone
test.explain: Initial receptor stimulation raises LH and testosterone before suppression.

test.q: Which drug lowers testosterone without a flare?
test.explain: Degarelix is a GnRH antagonist; it blocks the receptor directly.

test.q: Why might bicalutamide be started before leuprolide?
choices: To block the effects of the testosterone flare
test.explain: An AR antagonist prevents the flare from worsening bone pain or cord compression.

test.q: Which condition is treated with a GnRH agonist to pause early puberty?
choices: Peripheral precocious puberty from an ovarian cyst
test.explain: Central precocious puberty is GnRH-driven, so suppressing the axis stops it.

test.q: Relugolix differs from degarelix because relugolix is:
test.explain: Relugolix is an oral nonpeptide GnRH antagonist.

test.q: A main long-term side effect of GnRH suppression is:
test.explain: Low gonadal steroids accelerate bone resorption.

test.q: GnRH is released from which brain region?
test.explain: GnRH neurons in the hypothalamus release GnRH into the portal blood to the pituitary.

test.q: Fast GnRH pulses favor ___ release; slow pulses favor FSH.
test.explain: Pulse frequency decoding shapes the LH/FSH ratio.

test.q: What is the low-hormone treatment added to long-term GnRH suppression to protect bone called?
test.explain: Add-back therapy limits bone loss and hot flashes.

test.q: In IVF, GnRH antagonists are used to:
test.explain: Blocking an early LH surge keeps follicles from ovulating too soon.

kidTest.q: GnRH from the brain normally comes in:
kidTest.explain: The brain taps out GnRH in beats.

kidTest.q: If GnRH is given nonstop, the gland:
kidTest.explain: Nonstop signals make the gland tune out.

kidTest.q: Doctors use these medicines to pause puberty that starts:
kidTest.explain: Very early puberty can be paused.

kidTest.q: Another medicine type covers the ___ so nobody hears it.
kidTest.explain: Antagonists block the receptor, like covering the drum.

kidTest.q: Where is the control center that sends GnRH?
kidTest.explain: The hypothalamus is in the brain.

advancedTest.q: A man with prostate cancer has spinal metastases and early leg weakness. Best hormonal approach while getting steroids and urgent spine assessment?
choices: Delay all hormonal therapy for months
advancedTest.explain: Antagonists suppress testosterone in days without a flare that could worsen cord compression.

advancedTest.q: Fezolinetant reduces menopausal hot flashes by:
choices: Blocking neurokinin 3 receptors on hypothalamic KNDy neurons
Blocking GnRH receptors on the pituitary
advancedTest.explain: NK3R antagonism quiets KNDy activity driving the heat-loss center.

advancedTest.q: A 6-year-old boy with central precocious puberty. Essential next step before treatment?
advancedTest.explain: Boys and young children with CPP need MRI to exclude hypothalamic lesions such as hamartomas.

lessons.title: Bone and Calcium Pharmacology

levels.kid: Your bones feel solid, but they are alive! Tiny workers are always fixing them. One team of workers digs away old bone, and another team builds new bone, like a road crew that tears up old road and lays fresh road. When we get older, the diggers can work faster than the builders, and bones get thin and break easily. This is called osteoporosis. Some medicines slow down the diggers. Other medicines speed up the builders. Bones also need calcium, the stuff in milk, and vitamin D, which your skin makes in sunlight, to stay strong.
levels.hs:
Bone is constantly **remodeled**. **Osteoclasts** break down (resorb) bone, and **osteoblasts** build new bone. In **osteoporosis**, resorption outpaces formation, so bones become fragile and fracture easily, especially the hip, spine and wrist.

**Calcium control:** parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises blood calcium by pulling it from bone and helping the kidneys and gut save more. Vitamin D increases calcium absorption from the gut.

**Drugs that slow resorption (antiresorptives):**
- **Bisphosphonates** (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid) stick to bone and poison osteoclasts. Oral ones must be taken with a full glass of water, sitting upright, on an empty stomach, because they irritate the esophagus.
- **Denosumab** is an antibody that blocks RANKL, a signal osteoclasts need to form.

**Drugs that build bone (anabolics):**
- **Teriparatide** and **abaloparatide** are PTH-like drugs. Given in short daily pulses, they build bone instead of breaking it down.
- **Romosozumab** blocks sclerostin, a brake on bone formation.

**Rare but serious side effects** of antiresorptives: jaw bone death (osteonecrosis of the jaw) and unusual thigh bone fractures.
levels.college:
**Remodeling biology.** Osteoblast lineage cells express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive differentiation and activation; osteoprotegerin (OPG) is a decoy receptor. Osteocytes secrete sclerostin, which inhibits Wnt signaling through LRP5/6, restraining osteoblasts.

**Bisphosphonates.** P-C-P analogs of pyrophosphate bind hydroxyapatite, especially at active resorption sites, and are taken up by osteoclasts. Nitrogen-containing agents (alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate, zoledronic acid) inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway, blocking prenylation of small GTPases (Ras, Rho, Rab) needed for the ruffled border, causing osteoclast apoptosis. Oral bioavailability is very low and blocked by food, calcium and iron. They are renally cleared and avoided in significant renal impairment. Zoledronic acid infusion can cause an acute-phase reaction (fever, myalgia) and hypocalcemia.

**Denosumab.** Fully human anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody, given subcutaneously every six months; not renally cleared. It does not bind bone, so its effect wears off quickly: stopping it causes rebound resorption and multiple vertebral fractures unless a bisphosphonate follows.

**Anabolics.** Intermittent PTH receptor (PTH1R) activation by teriparatide (PTH 1–34) or abaloparatide (PTHrP analog) favors formation over resorption (the anabolic window). Continuous PTH causes net resorption, as in hyperparathyroidism. Romosozumab (anti-sclerostin) increases formation and decreases resorption, but it carries a boxed warning for myocardial infarction and stroke. Anabolic therapy must be followed by an antiresorptive to keep gains.

**Other calcium drugs.** Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic that sensitizes the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells, lowering PTH in secondary and some primary hyperparathyroidism. Calcitriol (active vitamin D) is used when renal 1α-hydroxylation fails. Calcitonin has weak antifracture efficacy.
levels.phd:
**Why bisphosphonates persist.** Affinity for hydroxyapatite varies (zoledronic acid highest), so skeletal retention lasts years and recycles after release during remodeling. This creates a long tail of effect that justifies drug holidays after several years in lower-risk patients, but also contributes to suppressed remodeling at sites of microdamage, the hypothesized mechanism of atypical femoral fractures: lateral cortical stress fractures that fail to heal because targeted repair is impaired. Femoral geometry and ancestry also influence risk.

**Osteonecrosis of the jaw.** The jaw has high remodeling and frequent microtrauma and infection through the dental mucosa. Proposed mechanisms include suppressed remodeling, antiangiogenic effects, soft-tissue toxicity and impaired immunity. It occurs with both bisphosphonates and denosumab and is much more common at oncology exposures than osteoporosis exposures.

**Denosumab rebound.** On withdrawal, osteoclast precursors that accumulated under RANKL blockade differentiate rapidly, producing a surge in turnover markers above baseline. Recent work suggests RANKL inhibition generates osteomorphs, recyclable osteoclast daughter cells that fuse back into active osteoclasts once RANKL returns, a cellular explanation for the rebound.

**Anabolic window.** Intermittent PTH1R activation favors osteoblast survival and Wnt activation (in part by suppressing sclerostin), while sustained activation raises RANKL. Abaloparatide preferentially binds the RG conformation of PTH1R, giving more transient cAMP signaling and less hypercalcemia. Osteosarcoma in rats at high prolonged exposure led to historic duration limits, which have since been relaxed.

**Genetics.** Sclerosteosis (SOST loss of function) produces very dense bone, the human genetic validation behind romosozumab. Activating LRP5 mutations cause high bone mass, and inactivating LRP5 mutations cause osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.
levels.expert:
**Treatment selection.** Fracture risk drives therapy, using bone density T-scores, prior fragility fractures and tools such as FRAX. Very high risk (a recent vertebral fracture, multiple fractures, a very low T-score) often justifies starting with an anabolic agent, then consolidating with an antiresorptive. Most others start with a bisphosphonate.

**Before starting antiresorptives.**
- Correct vitamin D deficiency and confirm normal calcium; denosumab and zoledronic acid can cause significant hypocalcemia, particularly in advanced kidney disease (measure calcium in mmol/L and recheck after the first dose in high-risk patients).
- A dental assessment before high-exposure oncology regimens, and good oral hygiene for everyone.
- Check renal function: bisphosphonates are avoided with low eGFR; denosumab is an option but hypocalcemia risk is higher.

**Pitfalls.**
- **Never just stop denosumab.** Plan a bisphosphonate transition to prevent rebound vertebral fractures.
- Teach oral bisphosphonate administration: empty stomach, plain water, upright for a while afterward. Esophagitis comes from tablets lodging in the esophagus.
- New thigh or groin pain on long-term antiresorptive therapy needs imaging of both femurs to look for atypical fracture.
- Check for secondary causes: glucocorticoids, hyperthyroidism, hypogonadism (including from ADT or aromatase inhibitors), celiac disease, myeloma, hyperparathyroidism.

**Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis** is the most common secondary form; fracture risk rises early in therapy. Neurosurgical and neurology patients on long steroid courses (brain tumor edema, myasthenia) deserve bone protection.

**Spine surgery link.** Osteoporosis increases screw loosening and fusion failure; some spine surgeons optimize bone with an anabolic agent before elective fusion.

keyPoints: Osteoclasts resorb; osteoblasts form; RANKL drives osteoclasts; sclerostin brakes osteoblasts
Nitrogen bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in osteoclasts
Denosumab blocks RANKL; stopping it causes rebound vertebral fractures
Intermittent PTH analogs (teriparatide) are anabolic; continuous PTH resorbs bone
Romosozumab blocks sclerostin; boxed warning for MI and stroke
Rare antiresorptive risks: osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fractures

test.q: Which cell breaks down bone?
test.explain: Osteoclasts resorb bone; osteoblasts build it.

test.q: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit which enzyme?
test.explain: Blocking FPP synthase prevents GTPase prenylation and kills osteoclasts.

test.q: Denosumab targets:
test.explain: It is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL.

test.q: What happens if denosumab is stopped without follow-on therapy?
choices: Rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures
test.explain: Its effect wears off fast; a bisphosphonate should follow.

test.q: Teriparatide builds bone because it is given:
test.explain: Intermittent PTH receptor activation favors formation; continuous activation favors resorption.

test.q: Why are oral bisphosphonates taken upright with plain water?
choices: To prevent esophageal irritation and allow absorption
test.explain: Lodged tablets cause esophagitis, and food blocks their poor absorption.

test.q: Romosozumab carries a warning for:
test.explain: Its boxed warning reflects increased cardiovascular events in a trial.

test.q: Name the osteocyte protein that romosozumab blocks.
test.explain: Sclerostin inhibits Wnt signaling and bone formation.

test.q: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic acting on the calcium-___ receptor.
test.explain: It sensitizes the CaSR, lowering PTH secretion.

test.q: Rare antiresorptive side effect: osteonecrosis of the ___ (one word).
test.explain: Osteonecrosis of the jaw occurs with bisphosphonates and denosumab.

test.q: Which secondary cause of osteoporosis is most common?
test.explain: Glucocorticoids suppress osteoblasts and raise fracture risk early.

kidTest.q: Are bones alive?
choices: Yes, workers fix them all the time
kidTest.explain: Bone cells constantly remodel bone.

kidTest.q: When bones get thin and break easily, it is called:
kidTest.explain: Osteoporosis means weak, thin bones.

kidTest.q: Some bone medicines work by:
kidTest.explain: Antiresorptives slow the cells that dig away bone.

kidTest.q: Your skin makes vitamin ___ in sunlight.
kidTest.explain: Vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium.

kidTest.q: Which helps bones stay strong?
kidTest.explain: Calcium is a building material for bone.

advancedTest.q: A patient on long-term alendronate develops dull thigh pain. Next step?
choices: Imaging of both femurs for atypical fracture
advancedTest.explain: Prodromal thigh pain can herald atypical femoral fractures, often bilateral.

advancedTest.q: Why does abaloparatide cause less hypercalcemia than teriparatide?
choices: It favors a PTH1R conformation with more transient cAMP signaling
It is excreted unchanged in bile
advancedTest.explain: Preferential RG-state binding gives briefer signaling.

advancedTest.q: A patient with advanced kidney disease receives denosumab. Main early risk to monitor?
advancedTest.explain: Blocking resorption in patients with impaired calcium handling can cause severe hypocalcemia.
